stem:
**Living standards in Kalinda** (a fictional country)

Kalinda is a small, open economy that exports tea, timber and cut flowers. Over the last three years the government has encouraged investment in these industries, and the statistics office reports that the economy has grown steadily. Employers say that business confidence is high and that they are hiring more workers.

However, many households report that their living costs have risen. The statistics office measures the price of a basket of goods and services bought by a typical household to construct a consumer price index. The weights are based on a survey of household spending ten years ago, when food made up 30% of the average budget. Today a household on a low income spends about half of its budget on food, and food prices have risen faster than the prices of other goods. In addition, the office has not been able to collect prices from the informal markets where many poorer households shop.

The government says that the figures show a success: nominal GDP has risen by 37.5% over the two years since Year 1. A trade union replies that this overlooks inflation and that the average wage has not kept up with prices. An economist points out that the GDP deflator, which covers all goods and services produced in the economy, and the consumer price index measure different things, and that neither shows how income is distributed. She adds that GDP does not include unpaid work in the home or the value of food grown by farming families for their own use.

**Table 1: Selected data for Kalinda (illustrative data)**

|  | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Consumer price index (Year 1 = 100) | 100 | 108 | 117 |
| GDP deflator (Year 1 = 100) | 100 | 105 | 125 |
| Nominal GDP (US\$ million) | 2,400 | 2,646 | 3,300 |
| Average monthly wage (US\$) | 310 | 330 | 349 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which index measures the average change in the prices of goods and services bought by typical households?

options.rationale: The deflator covers all goods and services produced in the economy.
Nominal GDP is not a price index.
Correct: it is based on a weighted basket of household purchases.

options.content: The index of the average wage
options.rationale: A wage index measures pay, not prices.

parts.explanation: The consumer price index measures prices of the household basket; the GDP deflator covers all output.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of inflation in Year 3 using the consumer price index, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: (117 − 108) ÷ 108 × 100 = 8.3%. (17% is the rise above the base year; 8.1% divides by the new index.)
parts.workedSolution: 1. (117 − 108) ÷ 108 × 100 = 8.3%. (17% is the rise above the base year; 8.1% divides by the new index.)

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the average monthly wage in Year 3 in Year 1 prices, in US\$ (to the nearest cent).

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage growth of real GDP between Year 2 and Year 3, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the growth of nominal GDP overstates the growth of the economy's output.

points.description: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, so it rises when prices rise even if output does not.
Between Year 1 and Year 3 the GDP deflator rose by 25%, so much of the 37.5% rise in nominal GDP is due to higher prices.
Real GDP, which removes the effect of price changes, rose by only 10% (from 2,400 to 2,640).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, so it rises when prices rise even if output does not. Between Year 1 and Year 3 the GDP deflator rose by 25%, so a large part of the 37.5% rise in nominal GDP is due to higher prices. Real GDP, which removes the effect of price changes, rose by only 10%, from US\$2,400 million to US\$2,640 million.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Analyse why the consumer price index may understate the inflation experienced by a low-income household in Kalinda.

points.description: The CPI uses weights from a survey ten years ago, when food was 30% of the budget.
A low-income household now spends about half of its budget on food, so food should have a larger weight for that household.
Food prices have risen faster than other prices, so the household's own inflation rate is higher than the CPI.
The statistics office could not collect prices in the informal markets where poorer households shop, so the index may miss price rises they face.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The CPI uses weights from a survey ten years ago, when food was 30% of the average budget, but a low-income household now spends about half of its budget on food. Food prices have risen faster than other prices, so food should carry a larger weight for that household and its own inflation rate is higher than the CPI shows. The statistics office also could not collect prices in the informal markets where poorer households shop, so the index may miss price rises they face.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Assess whether the data in Table 1 show that people in Kalinda are better off in Year 3 than in Year 1.

points.description: Real GDP rose by 10% (from 2,400 to 2,640), which suggests that output has increased.
The average real wage fell between Year 2 and Year 3 (from US\$305.56 to US\$298.29) and was below the Year 1 level of US\$310, so workers' purchasing power has declined.
The CPI may understate the inflation for poor households, so their real incomes may have fallen further.
GDP excludes unpaid and subsistence work and the informal sector, so living standards may be understated in some respects.
GDP and the average wage say nothing about how income is distributed.
A justified judgement, for example that output has grown but the data do not show that typical households are better off.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, developed and applied to the data, with a supported judgement.
Some development of one side or limited use of the data.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Real GDP rose by 10% between Year 1 and Year 3, from US\$2,400 million to US\$2,640 million, which shows that output has increased and supports the government's claim. However, the average real wage fell from US\$305.56 in Year 2 to US\$298.29 in Year 3, below the Year 1 level of US\$310, so workers' purchasing power has declined. The CPI may also understate inflation for low-income households, which spend more on food, so their real incomes may have fallen further. On the other hand, GDP excludes unpaid and subsistence work and the informal sector, so some improvements may be missed, and neither GDP nor the average wage shows how income is distributed. Overall the data show growth in output but do not show that typical households are better off; real wages and the experience of poorer households suggest that many are not.

explanation: CPI measures household prices; inflation Year 3 8.3%; real wage Year 3 US\$298.29; real GDP growth 4.8%; nominal growth overstates real growth; weights and informal markets bias the CPI; output grew but real wages fell.
hints: Real value = nominal value ÷ price index × 100.
Inflation = change in the index ÷ earlier index × 100.
In (f) weigh GDP growth against the real wage and the limits of the data.

stem: A government wants to reduce the consumption of tobacco and to widen access to school education.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how the provision of information by the government could reduce the consumption of a demerit good such as tobacco.

points.description: Tobacco is a demerit good: consumers tend to underestimate the harm it does (imperfect information).
Health warnings and campaigns give accurate information about the costs of smoking.
Consumers' perceived benefit falls, so the demand curve shifts to the left.
Described diagram: price (US\$) on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis; demand shifts from D1 to D2, and price and quantity fall.
Quantity moves closer to the social optimum, since smoking also imposes external costs on others.
Information can change attitudes and habits over the long run, especially among the young.
It leaves choice with consumers.
It is cheap relative to bans or taxes and needs little enforcement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Tobacco is a demerit good because consumers tend to underestimate the harm it does, which is a problem of imperfect information. Health warnings and campaigns give accurate information about the health costs of smoking, so consumers value tobacco less. With price (US\$) on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, the demand curve shifts to the left from D1 to D2, so the equilibrium price and quantity fall. The quantity moves closer to the social optimum, since smoking also imposes external costs on others through smoke and health-care costs. Information can change attitudes and habits over the long run, especially among the young, it leaves the choice with consumers, and it is cheap relative to bans or taxes, with little need for enforcement.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Assess whether direct provision of school education by the government is the best way of ensuring that all children are educated.

points.description: Education is a merit good with external benefits, so the market would under-provide it.
Direct provision, financed by taxation, gives access to children from poor families, improving equity.
More education raises productivity and growth, benefiting the economy as a whole.
There is an opportunity cost: the money could be spent on other priorities.
The service must be financed from taxes or borrowing, which may be limited.
Without competition or a profit motive, costs may be high and quality may be low (X-inefficiency).
Demand may exceed supply, causing overcrowded classes and rationing.
Alternatives include subsidies or vouchers to private or church-run schools, so the government finances without producing.
Information campaigns and conditional grants can raise demand for education among families who underestimate its benefits.
The success of direct provision depends on management, teacher training and the capacity of institutions.
Compared with alternatives, direct provision is simple and guarantees access, but alternatives may be more efficient.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed, balanced analysis applied to the question, with evaluation and a supported judgement.
Some analysis and application; evaluation limited or judgement not supported.
Simple, undeveloped points with little application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Education is a merit good with external benefits, so a free market would under-provide it, particularly for poor families. Direct provision financed by taxation gives access to all children, improving equity, and a more educated population raises productivity and growth. However, there is an opportunity cost, because the money could be spent elsewhere, and the service has to be financed from taxes or borrowing, which may be limited. Without competition or a profit motive, costs may be high and quality low, and if demand exceeds supply classes become overcrowded. Alternatives include subsidies or vouchers for private or church-run schools, so that the government finances education without producing it, and information campaigns or conditional grants can raise demand among families that underestimate the benefits. Direct provision is simple and guarantees access, but alternatives may be more efficient, and its success depends on management, teacher training and the capacity of institutions. Overall, state provision is the most reliable way of making primary education universal in a low-income country, but the government should use alternatives where they improve quality or reduce cost.

explanation: (a) Information corrects underestimated harm, shifts demand left and moves quantity towards the social optimum. (b) Direct provision: external benefits and equity against opportunity cost, X-inefficiency and alternatives.
hints: In (a) describe the shift of demand and the change in output relative to the social optimum.
In (b) weigh external benefits and equity against opportunity cost and efficiency, then judge.

stem: The price of imported oil rises sharply in an oil-importing economy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain, using an aggregate demand and aggregate supply diagram described in words, how the rise in oil prices could affect real output and the price level.

points.description: Oil is an input into production and transport, so firms' costs of production rise.
At each price level firms are willing to supply less output, so the short-run aggregate supply curve shifts to the left, from SRAS1 to SRAS2.
Described diagram: price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis; AD slopes downward, SRAS slopes upward, and equilibrium is where they cross.
The new equilibrium, where AD meets SRAS2, has a higher price level.
Real output is lower.
Employment falls as firms need fewer workers.
Higher prices with lower output and employment is stagflation (cost-push inflation).
Long-run aggregate supply is unchanged if the shock is temporary.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Oil is an input into production and transport, so a rise in its price raises firms' costs. At each price level firms are willing to supply less, so the short-run aggregate supply curve shifts to the left from SRAS1 to SRAS2. With the price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis, the downward-sloping AD curve crosses the upward-sloping SRAS curve at the initial equilibrium. After the shift, the new equilibrium, where AD meets SRAS2, has a higher price level and a lower level of real output. Employment falls as firms need fewer workers, so the economy experiences stagflation, that is, cost-push inflation with falling output. Long-run aggregate supply is unchanged if the shock is temporary.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Assess whether the government should respond to the oil price rise by increasing aggregate demand.

points.description: Increasing AD (for example by raising government spending or cutting taxes) shifts AD to the right.
Real output and employment would rise, reducing the fall caused by the shock.
The price level would rise further, since SRAS is upward-sloping, so inflation would be worse.
The problem is on the supply side, so demand policy treats the symptoms, not the cause.
If the shock is temporary, it may be better to allow the economy to adjust, since the price level may fall back.
Supply-side measures, such as energy efficiency, alternative energy or subsidies to transport, could shift SRAS back to the right.
The effect on output depends on how much spare capacity the economy has.
Higher AD raises imports, worsening the balance of payments, which is already under pressure from higher oil import costs.
Expansionary policy costs money and may add to the budget deficit and debt.
Time lags: policies take time to work and the shock may be over by then.
Inflation expectations may increase if prices keep rising, leading to wage demands.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed, balanced analysis applied to the question, with evaluation and a supported judgement.
Some analysis and application; evaluation limited or judgement not supported.
Simple, undeveloped points with little application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Increasing AD, for example by raising government spending or cutting taxes, would shift AD to the right and raise real output and employment, reducing the fall caused by the oil shock. However, since SRAS slopes upward, the price level would rise further, so inflation would be worse. The problem is on the supply side, so demand policy treats the symptoms, not the cause. If the shock is temporary, it may be better to allow the economy to adjust, as the price level may fall back when oil prices fall. Supply-side measures, such as improving energy efficiency, developing alternative energy or subsidising transport, could shift SRAS back to the right and reduce both inflation and unemployment. The effect on output also depends on how much spare capacity there is, and higher AD raises imports, worsening a balance of payments that is already under pressure from higher oil costs. Expansionary policy costs money and may add to the budget deficit, policies take time to work and higher inflation could raise inflation expectations. Overall the government should be cautious about increasing AD: it is justified only if unemployment is high and the shock is lasting, and it should be combined with supply-side measures.

explanation: (a) SRAS shifts left: higher price level, lower output and employment (stagflation). (b) Higher AD restores output but raises prices further; supply-side responses and the timing of the shock matter.
hints: In (a) describe the shift of SRAS and the new equilibrium.
In (b) say why increasing AD treats the symptoms and what it does to the price level.
